hints: Look for a plane of symmetry through each benzene ring and check which carbons can be swapped without changing the molecule.
Remember each set of chemically equivalent carbons gives one peak, so count unique ring carbon types plus unique carbonyl carbons separately.
walkthrough:
See what carbon-13 NMR counts**
Think of each peak as one unique carbon environment. If two carbons have exactly the same surroundings, they share a peak. Symmetry is the shortcut to spotting this.

Work through F**
$\text{HO}_2\text{C-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$ is 1,4-disubstituted with two identical $\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$ groups. The two carbonyl carbons are identical, giving 1 peak. In the ring, the two $\text{C-CO}_2\text{H}$ carbons are identical, and the remaining four $\text{CH}$ carbons form two identical pairs. That is 2 ring types + 1 carbonyl type = 3 peaks.

Work through G**
G has three different substituents, $\text{-NH}_2$, $\text{-NH}_2$ and $\text{-OH}$, in 1,3,4 positions, so there is no symmetry to make any ring carbons equivalent. All six ring carbons are in different environments, giving 6 peaks.

Final answer: F: 3 peaks
G: 6 peaks

hints: Pair each $\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$ group from F with an $\text{-NH}_2$ group from G and recall what small molecule is lost at each link.
Focus on how to draw $\text{-C(=O)-NH-}$ with all atoms and bonds shown, keeping the $\text{-OH}$ untouched on the G ring.
walkthrough:
Build the condensation link**
A carboxylic acid plus an amine gives an amide plus water: $\text{-COOH + H}_2\text{N-} \rightarrow \text{-CONH- + H}_2\text{O}$. Here F supplies two $\text{-COOH}$ ends and G supplies two $\text{-NH}_2$ ends, so two amide bonds form per repeat unit.

Draw the repeat unit correctly**
Join them as benzene(F) bonded to $\text{C(=O)}$, then to $\text{N(H)}$, then to benzene(G) carrying the $\text{OH}$ group, then to $\text{N(H)}$, then to $\text{C(=O)}$, then back to benzene(F). Show at least one $\text{-C(=O)-N(H)-}$ in full displayed form, with $\text{C=O}$ double bond and $\text{N-H}$ single bond drawn out. Add continuation bonds through the outer carbonyl carbons and outer nitrogens to show the polymer continues.

Final answer: Repeat unit: $\text{-CO-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-CO-NH-C}_6\text{H}_3\text{(OH)-NH-}$ with both amide links shown displayed as $\text{-C(=O)-N(H)-}$ and water eliminated. One repeat unit only, with continuation bonds at each end.

hints: Draw $\text{CH}_2\text{=CH}_2$ and label the $\text{C=C}$ double bond as one sigma plus one pi bond.
Think about what remains in poly(ethene) $\text{-[CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{]-}_n$ and what new bond joins one monomer to the next.
walkthrough:
Separate what breaks**
Each ethene has $\text{C=C}$ made of one $\sigma$ and one $\pi$ bond. During addition polymerisation the $\sigma$ framework stays, only the weaker $\pi$ bond of each $\text{C=C}$ breaks to free two electrons for new links.

See what forms**
Those freed electrons form new $\text{C-C}$ single bonds between monomer units along the chain. A single bond is a $\sigma$ bond only, so only $\sigma$ bonds are formed. No new $\pi$ bonds are created.

Final answer: bonds broken: pi-bonds only (tick)
bonds formed: sigma-bonds only (tick)

hints: Convert each $\text{C=C}$ into a $\text{-CH-CH-}$ saturated unit by adding one bond to each carbon along the chain.
Remember propene gives a $\text{-CH}_2\text{-CH(CH}_3\text{)-}$ unit and phenylethene gives a $\text{-CH}_2\text{-CH(C}_6\text{H}_5\text{)-}$ unit, joined together in one chain.
walkthrough:
Open each double bond**
For addition polymers, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CH}_2$ becomes $\text{-CH}_2\text{-CH(CH}_3\text{)-}$ and $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH=CH}_2$ becomes $\text{-CH}_2\text{-CH(C}_6\text{H}_5\text{)-}$. The substituents $\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5$ stay attached to one carbon of each unit.

Join one of each together**
Link the two saturated units end to end to make a four carbon backbone, for example $\text{-CH}_2\text{-CH(CH}_3\text{)-CH}_2\text{-CH(C}_6\text{H}_5\text{)-}$. Put a short continuation bond through the end $\text{CH}_2$ and the end $\text{CH}$ to show the chain continues beyond this section.

Final answer: $\text{-CH}_2\text{-CH(CH}_3\text{)-CH}_2\text{-CH(C}_6\text{H}_5\text{)-}$ (order of the two monomer units may be reversed) with continuation bonds at both ends of the four-carbon chain.

hints: Look at the backbone of a polyalkenes chain and decide whether the $\text{C-C}$ and $\text{C-H}$ bonds have a significant dipole for water or enzymes to attack.
walkthrough:
Link polarity to hydrolysis**
Hydrolysis needs a polar bond, such as $\text{C=O}$ in a polyester or polyamide, where $\delta+$ carbon can be attacked by water. Polyalkenes like poly(ethene) have only $\text{C-C}$ and $\text{C-H}$ single bonds which are essentially non-polar with no $\delta+$ centre, so water cannot break the chain and biodegradation is very slow.
Final answer: The polymer backbone contains only non-polar $\text{C-C}$ (and $\text{C-H}$) bonds with no dipole, so they are not susceptible to attack by water / hydrolysis.

hints: Think of one route that breaks polar links in the chain using water with help from reagents or biological catalysts.
Think of a second route that uses light energy to break bonds by radical formation, often helped by $\text{C=O}$ groups in the chain.
walkthrough:
Water based breakdown**
Polymers with hydrolysable links such as esters or amides can be split by hydrolysis with dilute acid or alkali, or by enzymes in microorganisms, breaking the long chain into smaller soluble molecules.

Light based breakdown**
UV light provides enough energy to break covalent bonds by radical mechanisms, causing the chain to fragment. This photodegradation is a separate environmental route from hydrolysis.

Final answer: 1. Hydrolysis by aqueous acid / alkali or by enzymes / bacteria.
2. Degradation / bond breaking by UV light (photodegradation).
